items.title: The square root of 2 cannot be written as a fraction
items.claim: Diagonal of a unit square has length root 2. The Pythagoreans believed all lengths were ratios of whole numbers. Hippasus showed root 2 wasn't. Legend says the Pythagoreans drowned him for revealing it.
items.prompt: Sketch the proof that root 2 is irrational.

options.text: It has too many decimal places

Assume root 2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then 2b squared = a squared, so a is even (say a = 2c). Then 2b squared = 4c squared, so b squared = 2c squared, so b is even. But a and b were lowest terms — contradiction
Because computers can't store it exactly

items.reveal:
The Pythagorean brotherhood (c. 500 BC) believed numbers were the foundation of reality and that all measurable lengths could be expressed as ratios of integers.

Hippasus of Metapontum supposedly proved the diagonal of a square is not commensurable with its side. Different ancient sources say he drowned at sea — some say by accident, some say murdered by his fellow Pythagoreans for exposing the result.

The proof: suppose root 2 equals a/b in lowest terms. Squaring: 2 = a squared over b squared, so 2 b squared equals a squared. Hence a squared is even, so a is even (say a = 2c). Substituting: 2 b squared = 4 c squared, so b squared = 2 c squared, so b squared is even, so b is even. Both a and b are even — contradiction with 'lowest terms'.

The discovery that not all numbers are rational was a major shock; the Greeks came to call these new quantities 'incommensurable'. Modern mathematics calls them irrationals — and there are vastly more of them than rationals.
items.why: Numbers feel like they should always be expressible as ratios. The very first geometric constructions reveal they're not.

items.title: In London, there are at least two people with exactly the same number of hairs
items.claim: Humans have at most about 150,000 hairs on their heads. London has over 9 million people. By the pigeonhole principle, at least 60 Londoners share an EXACT hair count.

options.text: If you put more than n items into n containers, at least one container has at least 2 items; more generally, if k*n + 1 items go into n containers, some container has at least k + 1

items.reveal:
The pigeonhole principle (Dirichlet's drawer principle, 1834): if you put n + 1 objects into n boxes, at least one box has at least 2 objects.

Applied to London: ~9 million heads, at most ~150,000 possible hair counts. 9 million divided by 150,000 = 60. So at least 60 Londoners share a hair count exactly.

Elegant applications:
- In any group of 367 people, two share a birthday (366 possible birthdays + leap year).
- Among any 6 people, three are mutual friends or three mutual strangers (a Ramsey theory result, R(3,3) = 6).
- Among any 10 distinct integers from 1 to 100, two have a sum or difference divisible by 17.
- In any sequence of n squared + 1 distinct real numbers, there is a monotone subsequence of length n+1 (Erdős-Szekeres).

The principle gives existence proofs without constructing the example. It's surprisingly powerful for such a simple idea.
items.why: The pigeonhole principle looks obvious but yields non-trivial results — existence guarantees from pure counting, often where direct construction is hopeless.

items.title: Your average speed never equals your speed at most moments
items.claim: Drive 60 miles in one hour at varying speeds — slowing for lights, accelerating onto highways. Average speed is 60 mph. But that doesn't mean you were doing 60 mph for most of the time. You may have spent more time at 30 mph than at 90 mph.
items.prompt: What's the difference between average and instantaneous?

options.text: Average and instantaneous are equal at the midpoint

Average speed = total distance / total time. Instantaneous speed = the limit of average speed over a vanishing interval — the derivative dx/dt. The mean value theorem guarantees at SOME instant the instantaneous speed equals the average, but not at most or all instants

items.reveal:
Mean Value Theorem (MVT): if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then there exists c in (a, b) such that f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a).

In driving terms: at SOME moment during your journey, your instantaneous speed was exactly equal to your average speed. (Not all moments — at least one.) This is the rigorous version of what intuition gets right.

Applications:
- Speed cameras using 'average speed enforcement': measure entry and exit times over a stretch; if average exceeds limit, you must have exceeded the limit at SOME moment (MVT). This is legally watertight.
- Optimisation: locating extrema where f'(c) = 0.
- L'Hopital's rule and Taylor's theorem are MVT consequences.

The full Taylor expansion exploits this: f(b) = f(a) + f'(a)(b-a) + (1/2)f''(a)(b-a)^2 + ... Each term corrects the linear approximation with higher-order behaviour. The remainder terms involve derivatives at intermediate points (Lagrange remainder).

Derivative as instantaneous rate: dx/dt at t = t_0 is the limit as h approaches 0 of (x(t_0 + h) - x(t_0)) / h. Defined when this limit exists. It tells you the rate of change exactly at time t_0 — not over any finite interval.

Velocity (vector) vs speed (scalar magnitude). At a U-turn, average velocity over the round trip is zero (you end up back where you started), but average speed is non-zero. Distinguishing them is key in kinematics.
items.why: Average rates feel like reliable summaries of what happened. The mean value theorem guarantees only ONE instant matches the average; for most of a journey, instantaneous speed differs. Speed limits use both.
